notes: Plain-language explanations keyed by axe-core rule ID. Written by hand for the mid-semester prototype (no live LLM). Impact is NOT stored here: it always comes from the live axe-core scan. Every entry stays 'pending_review' until a teammate checks it against sourceUrl with the review rubric.

image-alt.plainTitle: An image has no text description
image-alt.plainLanguageSummary: This image has no alternative (alt) text, so people who can't see it get no information about what it shows.
whoIsAffected: People browsing with images turned off
image-alt.whyItMatters: Screen readers read an image's alt text out loud. With no alt attribute, the screen reader may read the file name (like "IMG_4032.jpg") or skip the image, so the user misses what it means.
image-alt.suggestedFix: Add an alt attribute that describes what the image communicates, in a short phrase. If the image is only decoration, use an empty alt (alt="") so screen readers skip it.
image-alt.manualCheck: Scanly can tell alt text is missing, but not whether alt text you add is accurate. Read your alt text and ask: would someone who can't see the image understand its purpose?

color-contrast.plainTitle: Text is hard to read against its background
color-contrast.plainLanguageSummary: The text color is too close to the background color, which makes it hard to read.
color-contrast.needsReviewSummary: Scanly couldn't measure this text's contrast automatically, often because it sits on a background image or gradient. Check by eye or with a contrast checker whether the text is easy to read.
whoIsAffected: Anyone reading on a phone in bright light
color-contrast.whyItMatters: Text needs enough contrast with its background to be readable. WCAG sets a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.
color-contrast.suggestedFix: Make the text darker or the background lighter (or the reverse) until the contrast ratio meets the minimum. Check your new colors with a contrast checker before you commit them.

exampleFix.before: .event-date { color: #999999; } /* on white: about 2.8:1, too low */

label.plainTitle: A form field has no label
label.plainLanguageSummary: This form field has no label connected to it, so assistive technology can't announce what the field is for.
label.whyItMatters: When a screen reader reaches an unlabeled field, it may only say "edit text," with no hint of what to type. Without a label, someone can't reliably fill in the form.
label.suggestedFix: Add a <label> element and connect it to the field by making the label's for attribute match the field's id. Placeholder text alone is not a label, because it disappears when you start typing.

button-name.plainLanguageSummary: This button has no text or label that says what it does, so assistive technology announces it as just "button."
button-name.whyItMatters: Icon-only buttons (like a magnifying glass or an X) look clear on screen, but a screen reader can't describe the icon. Users hear "button" and have to guess what pressing it will do.
button-name.suggestedFix: Put visible text inside the button. If the button must show only an icon, add an aria-label that says what it does.

link-name.plainLanguageSummary: This link has no text that says where it goes, so assistive technology can't tell users its purpose.
link-name.whyItMatters: Screen-reader users often jump from link to link to find what they need. A link with no text may be read as just "link" or as a long web address, so they can't tell where it leads.
link-name.suggestedFix: Give the link visible text that describes where it goes. For an image or icon link (like a social media icon), add alt text to the image or an aria-label to the link.

html-has-lang.plainTitle: The page doesn't say what language it's in
html-has-lang.plainLanguageSummary: The page is missing a lang attribute, so screen readers have to guess which language to read it in.
html-has-lang.whyItMatters: Screen readers use the page language to choose the right pronunciation. If they guess wrong, English text may be read with another language's rules and become hard to understand.
html-has-lang.suggestedFix: Add a lang attribute to the <html> tag at the top of the page, using the page's main language code (for example, "en" for English).
html-has-lang.manualCheck: Make sure the language code matches the language the page is actually written in.

document-title.plainLanguageSummary: The page is missing a <title>, so its browser tab and bookmarks have no name.
document-title.whyItMatters: The page title is the first thing a screen reader announces when a page opens. Without one, users can't quickly tell which page they're on or tell open tabs apart.
document-title.suggestedFix: Add a short, unique <title> inside the <head> that describes the page, ideally with the page name first and the site name after.
document-title.manualCheck: Check that the title actually describes this page and is different from your site's other pages.

heading-order.plainLanguageSummary: The headings jump levels (for example, from a main heading straight to a third-level heading), which makes the page outline confusing.
heading-order.whyItMatters: Many screen-reader users move through a page by its headings, like a table of contents. A skipped level makes it look like a section is missing.
heading-order.suggestedFix: Use heading levels in order: one <h1> for the page, <h2> for main sections, <h3> inside those. Choose the level by structure, then use CSS to change how big it looks.
